Slides (black — the short unified 453 deck), the lecture notes (green — study guide written from Dr. Alqattan's lecture by Mohammed Alessa, Mohammed Alsalamah & Abdulrahman Alomar) and every gift (red). Aldughaither has no hand chapter. Many gifts test upper-limb nerve anatomy and hand infections that aren't on the slides — they are in section 5 with added background.

  • Hand Injuries — Plastic Surgery, 453 Surg Course.
  • Two halves: nerves that are squeezed or cut, and fractures that either sit still in a cast or need an operation.
CompressionLaceration (cut nerve)
OnsetGradual; comes and goes, then persistsImmediate, at the moment of injury
Numbness and weaknessBuild up; worse at night and with usePresent from day one
WastingAppears as compression becomes chronicDelayed: develops over the following months
The muscleStill receives signal, so it stays responsiveNo signal; stops responding after ~6 months
TreatmentConservative trial, then surgical decompression< 6 months: nerve repair · > 6 months: tendon transfer
  • Sensory map: median = radial 3½ digits · ulnar = ulnar 1½ digits · radial = only a small patch on the back of the hand (dorsal first web space) — most patients never notice it.

1. Median nerve — carpal tunnel syndrome

  • Signs and symptoms: numbness in the radial 3½ digits · more at night, with excessive use · wasting in the thenar muscles · weak thumb abduction.
  • Special manoeuvres: Phalen's · Tinel's. Investigation: nerve conduction study (NCS).
  • Treatment: lifestyle modification · splint at night · surgery (carpal tunnel release).

Tinel's sign (tapping over the carpal tunnel) and Phalen's test (wrists held in full flexion)

  • The most common nerve compression in the hand. Floor = carpal bones (hard), roof = transverse carpal ligament (hard); nothing can expand, so any extra pressure lands on the nerve.
  • Symptoms: numbness of thumb, index, middle and radial half of ring finger · worse at night · worse with sustained use (phone, driving) · drops things because they can't feel them. Signs: thenar wasting · weak thumb abduction (can't lift the thumb away from the palm) · progressive.
TestHowPositive result
Tinel's signTap over the median nerve at the carpal tunnelElectric tingling into the median distribution
Phalen's testHold the wrist in full flexion (reverse Phalen's: full extension)Symptoms within 30–60 seconds (normal person ~10 minutes)
Nerve conduction studyStimulate the median nerve across the wristSlowed conduction confirms compression
  • Treatment ladder: (1) lifestyle — wrist rest, neutral wrist, breaks · (2) night splint · (3) steroid injection (some surgeons — reduces swelling, not a cure) · (4) carpal tunnel decompression — the only definitive treatment.
  • Splint rules: a splint controls symptoms; it doesn't treat the compression — judge it after a 3-week trial; if lifestyle + splint fail → surgery. Compression never resolves by itself — it stabilises or worsens. Intermittent symptoms that settle with rest → conservative; constant, persistent symptoms → decompression.
  • Goals of surgery: prevent further deterioration and give the nerve a chance to recover. In very chronic severe cases recovery may be incomplete — manage expectations.
  • Numbness of thumb, index and middle fingers, weak thumb opposition, positive Tinel's → carpal tunnel syndrome. 441
  • Complete median nerve transection at the wrist — expected loss → abduction of the thumb. 432 ×2
  • Same scenario with both thumb abduction and opposition offered → thumb opposition (completely lost; abduction partly kept by abductor pollicis longus). 437 ×4

2. Ulnar nerve — cubital tunnel syndrome

  • Signs and symptoms: numbness in the ulnar 1½ digits · weakness and difficulty with fine movement · wasting in the first web space · weak finger adduction/abduction · claw hand.
  • Special manoeuvres: Tinel's · Froment test. Investigation: NCS. Treatment: lifestyle modification · splint at night · surgery (cubital tunnel release).
  • Same story as the median nerve, but the squeeze is at the elbow. Loss of fine movements — writing, doing their hair, fastening a necklace. Tinel's at the elbow sends tingling into the ulnar fingers.
  • Median vs ulnar — listen to the complaint: carpal tunnel: "I keep dropping things" (sensory). Cubital tunnel: "I can't do fine tasks" (weak intrinsics).
  • Froment's test: grip paper between thumb and side of index, then pull. Normal: thumb stays straight (adductor pollicis + first dorsal interosseous — ulnar). Positive: thumb IP joint bends — flexor pollicis longus (median) takes over.
  • Classic ulnar triad: claw hand + wasting of the first dorsal interosseous + positive Froment's. Confirm with NCS.
  • Treatment: stop leaning on the elbows (hard desks, studying in bed — classic in students at exam season) · night splint (a towel around the elbow keeps it straight) · surgical decompression if both fail.
  • Ulnar laceration: numbness, weakness and clawing appear immediately; wasting delayed — acute → nerve repair, late → tendon transfer. Exam pattern: a median or ulnar scenario is almost always the tunnel (compression), not a laceration.
  • Claw hand after K-wire insertion at the elbow → ulnar nerve. 438 ×4

3. Radial nerve — radial tunnel syndrome (posterior interosseous nerve)

  • Signs and symptoms: pain and weakness in wrist and finger extension without sensory involvement. Investigation: NCS. Treatment: surgery (the slide says "cubital tunnel release" — it means radial tunnel release, as in the notes).
  • Mostly a motor nerve, and its problems usually come from injury rather than compression. Extends the wrist, fingers and thumb; sensation only to a small dorsal patch.
  • Textbook nuance: the PIN branches after the nerve to extensor carpi radialis longus, so pure PIN compression gives finger and thumb drop with wrist extension preserved (wrist deviates radially). A full wrist drop points to a higher lesion (spiral groove).

Radial palsy after a humeral shaft fracture

  • The radial nerve wraps around the humerus in the spiral groove → injured by the fracture or during fixation. Key question: when did the wrist drop start? At the moment of injury → stretched/bruised (neurapraxia), expected to recover. Only after reduction or surgery → may be trapped or cut — more concerning, lower threshold to explore.
  • Management: most are conservative for the first 3 months; no recovery by 3 months → explore and repair; no recovery by 6 months → tendon transfer.
  • Humerus fracture, can't extend the fingers or wrist → radial nerve. 439 ×7
  • Radial head fracture, can't extend the digits but can extend the wrist and elbow, no sensory loss → posterior interosseous nerve. 438 ×2
MedianUlnarRadial
Compression siteCarpal tunnel (wrist)Cubital tunnel (elbow)Radial tunnel (forearm)
Sensory lossRadial 3½ digitsUlnar 1½ digitsSmall dorsal patch, rarely noticed
Key motor lossThumb abduction (thenar)Finger abduction/adduction; fine movementsWrist, finger and thumb extension
WastingThenar eminenceFirst dorsal interosseous—
Deformity—Claw handWrist drop
Patient says"I drop things"; worse at night"I can't write or do my hair""My hand falls"
Special testsTinel's (wrist), Phalen'sTinel's (elbow), Froment'sNCS
Typical causeCompressionCompressionTrauma: humeral shaft fracture

Nerve laceration — repair or transfer

  • Median or ulnar laceration: nerve repair within the first 6 months; tendon transfer after 6 months. Radial palsy after humeral fracture: observe → no recovery at 3 months: explore and repair → no recovery: tendon transfer.
  • Why 6 months? After a cut the muscle gets no stimulation; after > 6 months its "receiver" stops working — the muscle is alive but won't contract however well the nerve is repaired. Tendon transfer moves a working muscle's tendon to take over the lost action (e.g. thumb abduction after median injury) — you give up one function to regain another.

4. Hand fractures

  • Classification/description: open vs closed · spiral/oblique vs transverse · simple vs comminuted · extra- vs intra-articular · displaced vs non-displaced.

Fracture patterns (transverse, oblique, spiral, comminuted) and intra-articular fractures

  • Management: immobilization (splinting/cast) · closed reduction and immobilization · operative fixation: closed reduction and internal fixation · open reduction and internal fixation (ORIF).
  • Indications for operative management: multiple finger fractures · rotation/scissoring · instability · comminuted fractures.

Fixation — K-wires vs plate and screws

  • More of an orthopaedic topic. Cast vs splint: cast can't be removed, splint can — in the ED apply a cast so the patient can't take it off before the specialist sees them. Check the fingers stay parallel with the hand open and closed — function wins over a perfect X-ray.
  • Any one of the four words = operative fixation: multiple finger fractures (nothing holds the finger) · rotation/scissoring (finger crosses its neighbour on making a fist) · instability (slips after reduction) · comminution. Exam strategy: if any of them appears, pick the operation option.
K-wiresPlates and screws
TechniqueClosed: reduce, check on X-ray, drill a smooth wire acrossOpen: expose and reduce under direct vision
InvasivenessLess invasive, no scarLeaves a scar
HardwareWires stick out and are pulled out at ~6 weeksStays in (removal needs a second operation)
StabilityLess rigidStrong, anatomical fixation
RehabilitationMovement waits until wires are outEarlier mobilisation
  • Closed 5th metacarpal fracture with scissoring of the 4th and 5th digits → call the hand surgeon and book the OR. 437
  • Open fracture of the 4th and 5th metacarpals → external fixation and K-wires (operative). 437
Added explanationWhen a hand fracture is splinted, use the safe ("intrinsic-plus") position: wrist ~30° extension, MCP joints 60–90° flexion, IP joints straight — the collateral ligaments stay at full length, so the joints don't stiffen.
  • Metacarpal shaft fracture treated conservatively — splint position → PIP neutral, MCP 60° flexion, wrist 30° extension. 437
Added explanationScaphoid — the commonest carpal fracture: fall on an outstretched hand with anatomical snuffbox tenderness; may not show on the first X-ray → immobilize and re-image (or MRI); risk of avascular necrosis of the proximal pole.
  • Fall on an outstretched hand, fracture near the snuffbox → scaphoid. 436

5. Other hand & upper-limb questions asked

Nerves and roots

Added explanationAnterior interosseous nerve (branch of the median) — pure motor to FPL, FDP of index/middle and pronator quadratus → can't make the "OK" sign (pinches with straight thumb IP and index DIP), no sensory loss. Axillary nerve (shoulder dislocation/reduction) → loss of deltoid abduction and the "regimental badge" patch over the lateral upper arm.
  • Patient can't make the "OK" sign → anterior interosseous nerve. 439 ×5
  • After shoulder reduction: lost sensation over the lateral arm and arm abduction → axillary nerve. 438 ×6
Added explanationDermatomes and roots: C5 lateral arm (deltoid, shoulder abduction, biceps reflex) · C6 lateral forearm and thumb · C7 middle finger · C8 little finger · T1 medial forearm. Erb's palsy (C5–C6, birth injury) → "waiter's tip" posture: arm adducted and internally rotated, elbow extended, forearm pronated. Klumpke's (C8–T1) → claw hand.
  • Root supplying middle finger sensation → C7. 438 ×2
  • C5–C6 root injury — sensory loss → lateral aspect of the arm and forearm. 437
  • Weak shoulder abduction, numb lateral arm, weak biceps reflex → C5. 434 ×2
  • Newborn with a "waiter's tip" posture → Erb's palsy. 429

Tendons

Added explanationFDP inserts on the distal phalanx and is the only flexor of the DIP joint; FDS flexes the PIP. A cut over the middle phalanx/DIP that stops DIP flexion = FDP. Test FDP by holding the PIP straight and asking the patient to bend the fingertip.
  • Laceration at the DIP level (picture), can't flex the fingertip → flexor digitorum profundus. 437

Infections, burns & masses

Added explanationFlexor (septic) tenosynovitis — after a penetrating injury: Kanavel's signs — finger held flexed, fusiform swelling, tenderness along the tendon sheath, severe pain on passive extension → IV antibiotics and urgent surgical drainage/washout of the sheath. A felon is a pulp-space abscess of the fingertip.
  • Needle prick, then flexed swollen finger with severe pain on passive extension → septic tenosynovitis. 436
Added explanationHigh-voltage electrical injury — small skin burns hide extensive deep muscle necrosis → compartment syndrome (pain on passive stretch) even with palpable pulses → fasciotomy. Escharotomy releases only a constricting circumferential skin eschar.
  • Electrical injury, burns at the flexor creases, palmar pulses present, pain on passive finger motion → fasciotomy. 435 ×3
Added explanationGanglion — the commonest hand/wrist lump, typically on the dorsum of the wrist: smooth, firm to hard (tense), fixed to the joint capsule/tendon sheath, may vary in size and transilluminate; young adults, often women.
  • 24-year-old woman, smooth hard immobile 2 × 2 cm mass on the dorsum of the hand, pain on wrist flexion → ganglion. 435 ×3
